text: Silkscreen printing became a fine art medium partly through Anthony Velonis, who brought the technique into the mainstream while working for the Works Progress Administration. The art form came to be called the serigraph. At his own request, he was not publicly credited with coining that word. He experimented until he could print on glass, plastics and metal, which widened the field. He grew up in New York City and married Elizabeth Amidon. They had four children.

Girolamo dai Libri learned illumination from his father Francesco, a skilled illuminator, and most likely also attended Domenico Morone's workshop, where he befriended Morone's son Francesco. They later collaborated on several commissions. Already young he stood out for miniatures, especially for the convent of Santa Maria in Organo in Verona. Vasari says that at about 25 he astonished his contemporaries with a painting there. He also painted altarpieces in an early Renaissance style. He died in 1555.

Walter Crane argued for anti-authoritarian democratic socialism among British socialists and in the labour movement. He produced a large body of work. Some of it was apolitical, mostly illustrations for children's books and general-interest literature of the Victorian era, and some carried explicit political messages. He is considered one of the most influential and prolific children's book designers of his generation. He lived from 1845 to 1915.

Martin Schongauer was the most important printmaker north of the Alps before Dürer, who collected his work. He came from Colmar and was known to his contemporaries as Martin Schön, or pretty Martin. He seems to have had the family background and training in goldsmithing that was usual for early engravers. Most of his surviving production is 116 engravings, all with his monogram but none dated. They were well known in Germany and Italy. He died in 1491.

George Morland's publishers made much more money from his prints than he did, since a lot of his work was meant for reproduction. His early work followed Francis Wheatley, but after the 1790s he found his own style. His best compositions are rustic scenes of farms and hunting, smugglers and gypsies, and rich landscapes influenced by Dutch Golden Age painting. He drank heavily and lived a rackety life. He was enormously prolific, though quality suffered. He died at 41.

George Stubbs taught himself to paint, independently of the great artists of the 18th century like Reynolds and Gainsborough. He is best known for horses, but his output includes history paintings too. His greatest skill was painting animals, maybe because of his love and study of anatomy. His series on a lion attacking a horse are early and significant examples of Romanticism. He enjoyed royal patronage. Whistlejacket hangs in the National Gallery in London.

Foreign visitors on the Grand Tour poured into Rome, and Pompeo Batoni specialised in portraits of them. His sitters were mostly British and Anglo-Irish gentlemen, often shown with famous Italian landscapes behind. These portraits ended up in British private collections and spread the genre's popularity in Britain. He also painted numerous allegorical and mythological pictures, with solid technical knowledge. He lived from 1708 to 1787.

Peasants, soldiers and other lower-class people drinking, smoking, playing cards or fighting in taverns are the subjects that made Adriaen Brouwer an innovator of genre painting. He also helped develop the tronie, a head or facial study that explores varieties of expression. In his last year he painted a few landscapes of tragic intensity. He worked in Flanders and the Dutch Republic. He had an important influence on the next generation of Flemish and Dutch genre painters. He died in 1638.

Robert Duncanson, a free Black man in antebellum America, spent most of his career in Cincinnati and helped develop the Ohio River Valley landscape tradition. Thomas Cole and other American landscape artists inspired him, and he counts as a second-generation Hudson River School painter. He worked with the abolitionist community in America and England to support and promote his work. He is considered the first African-American artist to be known internationally. He died in 1872.

Franz Anton Maulbertsch studied at the Academy of Vienna. Through Paul Troger he came to know the Venetian painters Piazzetta and Pittoni. He studied Sebastiano Ricci's frescoes in the Schönbrunn Palace and spent time with Giambattista Tiepolo, who was in Würzburg from 1750. He was an appreciated frescoer, and most commissions were for churches. He painted in Rococo style in the German and Hungarian regions. He lived from 1724 to 1796.

Francesco Zuccarelli is considered the most important landscape painter to emerge from Venice in the mid-eighteenth century. His Arcadian views became popular across Europe, and especially in England, where he lived for two long periods. His patrons included the nobility. He often worked with other artists such as Antonio Visentini and Bernardo Bellotto. In 1768 he became a founding member of the Royal Academy. He died in 1788.

Bernhard Strigel came from Memmingen and probably studied with Zeitblom at Ulm. He was the most important member of a family of artists based in Memmingen. Emperor Maximilian I held him in high favor, and Strigel repeatedly travelled for him to Augsburg, Innsbruck and Vienna. His religious paintings include four altar wings in the Berlin Gallery and ten pictures of the Genealogy of Christ in Nuremberg. They are of less artistic value than his portraits. He died in 1528.

Ferdinand Bac came from a family tied to Napoleon: his father was an illegitimate nephew of the Emperor. As a young man he moved in the fashionable Paris of the Belle Époque and drew caricatures for popular journals. He travelled widely in Europe and the Mediterranean. In his fifties he began a second career as a landscape gardener. The gardens he made at Les Colombières in Menton are now a Monument Historique. He also wrote a lot.

For centuries nobody could attribute Giovanni Agostino da Lodi's works with confidence, until Bernard Berenson defined his style and career. One of his first identified pieces is the Boatmen Altarpiece in the church of San Pietro Martire at Murano. His only signed work is a pair of saints in the Brera, which shows Lombard influences such as Bramantino's. Leonardo's style influenced him later. He was active from about 1495 to 1525.

Rik Wouters made some 200 works in his 34 years. Illness killed him partway through the First World War, in Amsterdam. He was a sculptor, painter, draughtsman and etcher in a typically Fauvist style, and his art resembled that of Matisse, Cézanne and Derain. One writer says his work reflects warmth and tenderness. His paintings use many colours and brush strokes and often leave canvas unpainted.

Ilya Repin grew up in Chuguev, then part of Russia. He became one of the most famous artists in Russia in the 19th century. His major works include Barge Haulers on the Volga, Religious Procession in Kursk Province, Ivan the Terrible and His Son Ivan, and Reply of the Zaporozhian Cossacks. He also painted revealing portraits of Glinka, Mussorgsky, Pavel Tretyakov and Leo Tolstoy, with whom he had a long friendship. He died in 1930.

Louis Marcoussis studied law in Warsaw before attending the Kraków Academy of Fine Arts. He then moved to Paris to study under Jules Lefebvre at the Académie Julian. His first major exhibition was at the Salon d'Automne in 1905. In the cafes of Montmartre and Montparnasse he got to know artists and writers. Guillaume Apollinaire, who had Polish roots too, suggested his French name. He died in 1941.

James Longacre ran away to Philadelphia at twelve and became an apprentice in a bookstore. His artistic talent showed, and he was released to apprentice at an engraving firm. He struck out on his own in 1819, providing illustrations for popular biographies. From 1844 until his death he was the fourth chief engraver of the United States Mint. Best known for the Indian Head cent of 1859. He also designed the Shield nickel.

Jan van Kessel the Elder came from the Brueghel family, and many of his subjects took inspiration from his grandfather Jan Brueghel the Elder. He worked in Antwerp in the mid-17th century. He painted insects, flowers, marines, river landscapes, paradise landscapes and allegories, and also animals and genre scenes. His contemporaries prized his works highly. Daniel Seghers and Frans Snyders also inspired him. He died in 1679.

Kanzan Shimomura came from a family of hereditary Noh actors in Wakayama. At eight he moved to Tokyo and studied under Kanō Hōgai, and after Hōgai's death under Hashimoto Gahō. He graduated first in his class at the Tōkyō Bijutsu Gakkō and began teaching there in 1894. His real name was Shimomura Seizaburō. He painted in the nihonga style. He lived from 1873 to 1930.

While attending primary school in Prague, Miloš Jiránek lived with the poet Jaroslav Vrchlický and had access to a huge library. He picked up foreign languages easily and read many books in the original. His father was a landowner. In 1894 he studied at the Faculty of Arts at Charles University, and a year later moved to the Academy of Fine Arts. He painted as a Neo-Impressionist and wrote art criticism. He died in 1911.

Piercy Roberts published political and social caricatures from a print shop at 28 Middle Row, Holborn, between 1801 and 1806. He drew himself standing in the doorway with a crowd of onlookers. Most of his prints are caricatures, some after his own designs and some after George Moutard Woodward. He collaborated with Thomas Rowlandson on a pair of portraits of Josephine Beauharnais, now in the Royal Collection, and Napoleon, in the British Museum.

Tosa Mitsunori was the son of Tosa Mitsuyoshi and the father of Tosa Mitsuoki. He moved to Sakai in his youth and sometimes presented painted fans to the Sentō Imperial Palace, but he never received a court position. At about 52 he returned to Kyoto with his eldest son. He made many small works with gold backgrounds, in variegated paints, in the tradition of the Tosa school. He died in 1638.

William Derby learned drawing in Birmingham from Joseph Barber. In 1808 he moved to London, where he began by making reduced drawings for the plates of the Stafford Gallery, a four-volume set of engravings of the Marquess of Stafford's paintings. He went on to a career as a portrait and miniature painter, sometimes making watercolour copies of notable pictures. He lived from 1786 to 1847.

Antonin Moine started as a landscape painter and then became a sculptor. He had some success at the Salon in the early 1830s. From 1835 to 1840 he worked with Louis-Parfait Merlieux and Carle Elshoecht on sculptures for the fountains on the Place de la Concorde in Paris. He was born in Saint-Étienne. He worked in the French Romantic style and died in 1849.

Hippolyte Sebron began as a decorative painter and had his first exhibition at the Salon in 1825. In 1827, while decorating the new Théâtre de l'Ambigu-Comique, Louis Daguerre took him on as a student, and he became a collaborator on Daguerre's popular dioramas. He also studied with Léon Cogniet. He painted landscapes, cityscapes and portraits. He worked in photography and pastels too. He died in 1879.

Isabella Piccini learned etching and engraving from her father Giacomo, an etcher and engraver in Venice. He trained her in the style of the great masters, such as Rubens and Titian. In 1666 she became a Franciscan nun at the Convent of Santa Croce and changed her name from Elisabetta to Sister Isabella. Prominent Italians commissioned portraits and religious works from her. Giovanni Antonio Remondini distributed her prints.

Lluís Borrassà learned painting from his father Honorat. In 1380 he is first documented as a member of the court of John I of Aragon, who brought prominent artists there. In 1390 he set up a workshop in Barcelona that would be the city's largest until 1420. Ferrer Bassa influenced his style, and he in turn influenced Bernat Martorell. He is widely thought to have introduced International Gothic painting to Catalonia.

Pope Clement VI summoned Matteo Giovannetti to Avignon to decorate the Palais des Papes, and he led teams of painters from across Europe. He began painting the Saint-Martial chapel on 13 October 1344. People often link him with the school of Simone Martini because of similarities in style, though there is no evidence the two ever met. More likely he took up a Sienese style while he was being educated in Italy. He was born in Viterbo.

A general wares dealer fathered Adolf Kašpar, who studied at the Prague Academy under Maxmilián Pirner. His mentor was Hanuš Schwaiger, a famous Czech painter and children's book illustrator, who recommended him to the academy and influenced his life and art. In 1907 he married Jitka Řepková in Velehrad. He perfected his pieces by collecting information from Czech literature. He died in 1934 in Železná Ruda.

Sanford Gifford, the painter, had cradled baby Dora Wheeler in his arms at her parents' country house on Long Island. Dora grew up to be a portrait artist, muralist, designer and illustrator of books and magazines. She designed textiles for her mother Candace Wheeler's firm, the Associated Artists. Her portrait of Harriet Beecher Stowe is dated 1890. She was also known as Mrs. Boudinot Keith.

Ignacio Suárez Llanos moved to Madrid while still very young. There he began studying at the Real Academia de San Fernando, where his teachers included Bernardino Montañés and Federico de Madrazo. Later a Spanish government scholarship let him continue at the Spanish Academy in Rome. He took part regularly in the National Exhibition of Fine Arts from 1858. He painted portraits and made illustrations. He came from Gijón and died in Madrid in 1881.

Johan Hörner began his studies in Stockholm with Johan Henrik Scheffel. As a Pietist he faced serious discrimination there, so in 1734 he moved to Denmark and lodged with a carpenter in a largely Pietist district of Copenhagen. For a time he helped other self-exiled Swedes find refuge, but he came under scrutiny and moved to the countryside. He specialised in portraits. He died in 1763.

The portrait painter Vicente López Portaña was Miguel Parra Abril's brother-in-law. Parra studied with Benito Espinós at the School of Flowers and Ornamentation in Valencia, and the academy there named him Academician of Merit for flower painting in 1803. He became court painter to King Ferdinand VII. He is best known for portraits and still lifes, mostly floral. He died in Madrid in 1846.

Karel van Mander, who was Lucas de Heere's pupil, wrote the main source for his life, Het Schilder-Boeck. De Heere came from Ghent, the second son of a sculptor and a miniaturist. He worked as a painter and watercolorist, made prints, wrote a biography, plays and poems. His costume books and portraits are a valuable resource for knowledge of 16th-century fashion. He may have died in Paris in 1584. Maybe.

Rembrandt's first teacher was Jacob van Swanenburg of Leiden. Swanenburg's father was a painter and print designer who served several times as Leiden's mayor. Jacob spent a substantial part of his early career in Italy before returning home. He was known for city views, history paintings, Christian religious scenes and portraits, and he worked as an art dealer too. He died in Utrecht in 1638.

Pantaleon Szyndler took his first art lessons at the School of Fine Arts in Warsaw with Rafał Hadziewicz. A scholarship from a society for the encouragement of fine arts let him continue his studies abroad. From 1870 to 1873 he was enrolled at the Academy of Fine Arts in Munich. He painted in the Academic style and is known mainly for nudes, religious works and Orientalist paintings. A close friend of Cyprian Norwid. Some canvases were inspired by Polish Romantic poetry.

The ninth of fourteen children, Jakob Emanuel Handmann had a father who was a baker and later bailiff of Waldenburg. In his teens he apprenticed as a stucco plasterer and studied painting in Schaffhausen. He specialised in portraits, and one of them shows the mathematician Leonhard Euler. He was a contemporary of Anton Graff, Angelica Kauffman and Johann Heinrich Füssli. He came from Basel and died in 1781.

Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld got his first artistic education from his father Veit, a draughtsman, engraver and painter in Leipzig. His earliest known works are copies. As a young man he joined the Nazarene painters, who revived the florid Renaissance style in religious art. He painted chiefly Biblical subjects. He is remembered for his extensive Picture Bible and for his designs for stained glass windows in cathedrals. He lived from 1794 to 1872.

Colonel Robert Jacob Gordon served in the Dutch army and explored South Africa as a naturalist. His father was a Scottish major-general in the Dutch Scots Brigade. At ten he joined a light dragoons unit as a cadet, and six years later he enrolled at the University of Harderwijk to study humanities. After graduating he went back to the army. His drawings of animals, such as a chacma baboon and a black-backed jackal, are dated 1773.

Switzerland's national painter is what people have called Albert Anker, because his pictures of 19th-century Swiss rural life stayed popular. He was born in Ins, the son of a veterinarian who sat in the constituent assembly of the Canton of Bern. The family moved to Neuchâtel in 1836. There his sketching teacher was Frédéric-Wilhelm Moritz. He and the later artist Auguste Bachelin took private drawing lessons together. He was also an illustrator.

Charles Martin Hardie first worked as a carpenter in the family business. His relation by marriage to the painter John Pettie persuaded him to train as an artist at the Trustees' Academy in Edinburgh. He came from East Linton. He specialised in portraits of Robert Burns and Sir Walter Scott in imaginary historical scenes, and in paintings of Scottish country life. He died in 1916.

A very accomplished engraver, Johannes Wierix made prints after his own designs as well as after local and foreign artists. He also engraved on silver and ivory, and made miniature pen drawings. He came from Antwerp, the son of Anton Wierix I. With other members of the Wierix family he helped spread appreciation for Netherlandish art abroad and create art that supported the Catholic cause in the Southern Netherlands. He lived from 1549 to about 1620.

At first Max Slevogt painted dark, in the prevailing Munich style. He studied at the Munich Academy from 1885, and in Paris he attended the Académie Julian. He drew caricatures for the magazines Simplicissimus and Jugend. With Lovis Corinth and Max Liebermann he was one of the foremost representatives in Germany of the plein air style. He is best known for landscapes and also worked as an illustrator. He died in 1932.

David Klöcker Ehrenstrahl came from Hamburg and had eight siblings. In 1648 he went to Amsterdam to learn painting from Juriaen Jacobsze. Four years later he left and moved to Skokloster Castle in Sweden, at the request of the nobleman Carl Gustaf Wrangel. Later he studied in Italy and visited the courts of France and England. He became a Swedish nobleman and portrait painter.

A friend and rival of J. M. W. Turner, Thomas Girtin helped establish watercolour as a reputable art form. His father, a wealthy brushmaker of Huguenot descent, died while Thomas was a child, and his mother then married a pattern-draughtsman. He learned drawing as a boy and was apprenticed to the topographical watercolourist Edward Dayes. He worked as an etcher too. He died young.

Sebastiano Ricci was about the same age as Piazzetta and an elder contemporary of Tiepolo. He represents a late version of the vigorous and luminous Cortonesque grand manner of fresco painting in Venetian painting. His nephew Marco Ricci trained with him and became an innovator in landscape painting. He painted in the late Baroque. He was born in 1659 and died in 1734.

In his own time, Utagawa Kunisada's reputation far exceeded those of his contemporaries Hokusai, Hiroshige and Kuniyoshi. He is considered the most popular, prolific and commercially successful designer of ukiyo-e woodblock prints in 19th-century Japan. He was also known as Utagawa Toyokuni III. Born in 1786, he died on 12 January 1865.

Carlo Maratta was the leading painter in Rome in the second half of the 17th century. He painted frescoes and canvases in a wide range of genres, including history painting and portraits. He also drew. His clients in Rome included various popes. He is the leading representative of the classicizing style in the Italian Late Baroque. He lived from 1625 to 1713.

Étienne Carjat's iconic portrait of Arthur Rimbaud, taken in October 1871, is his best-known work. He worked as a journalist and caricaturist in Paris, and as a photographer. He co-founded the magazine Le Diogène and founded the review Le Boulevard. He made many portraits and caricatures of political, literary and artistic figures. Most of his photography cannot be traced, because it was sold to a Mr. Roth in 1923.

Born Henri-Edmond-Joseph Delacroix, Cross took his shorter name as a painter. He is most acclaimed as a master of Neo-Impressionism and played an important role in shaping the second phase of that movement. He was a significant influence on Matisse and many other artists. His work helped bring about Fauvism. He also made prints. He lived from 1856 to 1910.
